prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Editor's Note: Reese Witherspoon, the Academy Award-winning actress, is honorary chairman of the Avon Foundation and is employed by Avon Products as its global ambassador. Reese Witherspoon says she wants to banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. (CNN) -- Every three minutes in the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that statistic terrifying. I was never naïve about breast cancer, but hearing this statistic put it all into perspective.   Women close to me have battled the disease and are now soldiers in the greater fight against it. But the moment I heard "every three minutes," I felt vulnerable and scared as I realized that anyone is susceptible. The only way for me to ease my fears was to take action. I needed to educate myself and others on this disease. As the Honorary Chair for the Avon Foundation, I had resources at my fingertips. I had access to an entire organization that is dedicated to giving back to women and educating people. So I started asking, "What do I need to know?" It was through that curiosity that I found out the most important fact in breast cancer: Early detection saves lives. According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, there is a 97 percent five-year survival rate when breast cancer is caught before it spreads to other parts of the body. When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms, which is why women need to perform self-exams regularly and contact their doctor upon noticing even the smallest change. Of course talking about breast cancer and breast health is a personal thing. I too am a private person but encourage all women to break through their reservations and talk to their doctors and physicians. We must also banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who were diagnosed in their 20s, an age when most women are graduating from college and just starting their lives as full adults.  Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk » . Women in their 20s and 30s should have a clinical breast exam by a health professional at least once every three years and women 40 and older should have an exam every year. I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, myself, my children and future generations of women, so one day we will not have to be afraid of breast cancer. I began my fight by learning important first steps in breast cancer detection, and will not end my fight until every woman can stand together saying we are breast cancer free. More than anything else, I have faith -- faith we will find a cure. I saw this commitment in the faces of the women in Washington -- in the faces of the women walking and the women and men who stood on the sidelines encouraging the 3,500 participants to the finish line. I was cheering right along with them, screaming for action to find a cure.  Avon's next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

outputs.L1:
**Editor’s Note:** Academy Award-winning actress Reese Witherspoon serves as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation and is employed by Avon Products as its global ambassador. She is committed to dispelling the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer.

**(CNN) —** Every three minutes in the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that statistic terrifying. I was never naïve about breast cancer, but hearing “every three minutes” put the reality of the disease into perspective.

Women close to me have battled breast cancer and are now soldiers in the broader fight against it. But when I heard that phrase, I felt vulnerable and afraid as I realized that anyone can be affected. The only way I could ease my fears was to take action. I needed to educate myself—and others—about the disease.

As honorary chair of the Avon Foundation, I had resources at my fingertips and access to an entire organization dedicated to giving back to women and educating people. So I began asking, “What do I need to know?”

Through that curiosity, I discovered the most important fact about breast cancer: Early detection saves lives. According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, breast cancer has a 97 percent five-year survival rate when detected before it spreads to other parts of the body.

When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms. That is why women need to perform regular self-exams and contact their doctors upon noticing even the smallest change.

Of course, talking about breast cancer and breast health is deeply personal. I, too, am a private person, but I encourage all women to overcome their reservations and speak with their doctors and physicians.

We must also dispel the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who had been diagnosed in their 20s—an age when most women are graduating from college and just beginning their lives as full adults.

*Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »*

Women in their 20s and 30s should receive a clinical breast exam from a health professional at least once every three years, while women age 40 and older should have an exam every year.

I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, for myself, for my children, and for future generations of women, so that one day we will no longer have to fear breast cancer.

I began my fight by learning the essential first steps in breast cancer detection, and I will not stop until every woman can stand together and say that we are free from breast cancer.

Above all, I have faith—faith that we will find a cure. I saw that commitment in the faces of the women in Washington: in those who walked and in the women and men who stood along the sidelines, encouraging all 3,500 participants to reach the finish line. I cheered alongside them, calling for action to find a cure.

Avon’s next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.
outputs.L2:
**Editor’s Note:** Academy Award-winning actor Reese Witherspoon serves as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation and works for Avon Products as the company’s global ambassador. She is seeking to dispel the mistaken belief that breast cancer does not threaten younger women.

**(CNN) —** In the United States, one woman learns that she has breast cancer every three minutes. As a daughter, mother and woman, I am frightened by that number. Although I had always understood the seriousness of the disease, this statistic made its impact unmistakably clear.

Several women in my life have fought breast cancer and have since become advocates in the broader effort to defeat it. Yet hearing the phrase “every three minutes” made me recognize that no one is immune, leaving me feeling afraid and exposed.

Taking action was the only way I could reduce that fear. I decided that I had to learn more about breast cancer and help inform other people. As honorary chair of the Avon Foundation, I had immediate access to an organization committed to supporting women and increasing public awareness. I therefore began by asking what information I needed most.

My questions led me to the most crucial lesson about breast cancer: Finding it early can save lives. The Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade reports that when the disease is detected before reaching other areas of the body, the five-year survival rate is 97 percent.

Breast cancer generally causes no symptoms when it initially appears. For that reason, women should conduct regular self-examinations and speak with a doctor if they observe even a minor change.

Discussions about breast health and cancer can understandably feel deeply private. I value my own privacy as well, but I urge women to move beyond any discomfort and have these conversations with their doctors and other medical professionals.

We also need to eliminate the misconception that younger women face no breast cancer risk. During the Avon Walk in Washington, I met survivors who had received their diagnoses while in their 20s—a stage when many women are completing college and beginning their adult lives.

*Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »*

Women between the ages of 20 and 39 should receive a clinical breast examination from a healthcare professional at least once every three years. Beginning at age 40, women should be examined annually.

I am deeply committed to confronting this destructive illness. My efforts are for my mother, my children, future generations of women and myself, with the hope that someday breast cancer will no longer inspire fear.

My involvement started with learning the essential first steps for detecting the disease. I will continue until women everywhere can unite and declare that breast cancer has been eradicated.

Above all, I believe that a cure will be discovered. I witnessed that same determination in Washington: in the women taking part in the walk, and in the women and men along the route who encouraged all 3,500 participants as they moved toward the finish line. I joined their cheers, calling loudly for action that will lead to a cure.

Avon’s following walk is scheduled for October 4 and 5 in New York City.

Early detection is one of the most important factors in successful treatment. When breast cancer is identified before it has spread, the five-year survival rate is about 97 percent. However, breast cancer can develop without obvious symptoms, making regular attention to breast health essential. Women should perform routine self-exams, become familiar with how their breasts normally look and feel, and consult a doctor promptly if they notice any changes.

Breast cancer is not limited to older women; younger women can also be diagnosed with the disease. For that reason, women of every age should feel comfortable discussing breast health, personal risk factors, and appropriate screening measures with their healthcare providers. Education, open communication, and early action can help save lives.

## Early Detection Is an Act of Self-Care

As women, we’re often experts at taking care of everyone else. We remember appointments, answer late-night calls, and make sure the people we love have what they need. But caring for ourselves—including our breast health—deserves the same attention.

Breast cancer can affect women at many ages. Although routine mammograms are generally recommended beginning at age 40 for women at average risk, women in their 20s and 30s shouldn’t assume breast health is something to think about “later.” This is the time to learn your family history, understand your personal risk, and pay attention to changes in your body.

Know what is normal for you. If you notice a new lump, swelling, skin dimpling, nipple changes or discharge, persistent pain, or a change in the size or shape of a breast, contact a healthcare professional. Most breast changes are not cancer—but they deserve to be evaluated. Don’t let anyone, including yourself, dismiss a concern simply because you’re young.

Talk with your doctor about whether factors such as family history, inherited genetic mutations, previous chest radiation, or dense breasts place you at higher risk. Some women may need genetic counseling or earlier screening with mammography or breast MRI.

For women at average risk, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends mammograms every two years from ages 40 through 74. Other medical organizations recommend different schedules, so make the decision with a clinician who understands your health history.

I also want to acknowledge that access to screening and quality care is not equal. Black women are more likely to die from breast cancer than white women and are more likely to develop the disease at younger ages. We must advocate not only for ourselves, but also for systems in which every woman is heard, supported, and treated promptly.

Please schedule the appointment you’ve been postponing. Ask questions. Encourage your friends, sisters, mothers, and daughters to understand their risk. Early detection cannot prevent every breast cancer, but finding cancer sooner can expand treatment options and save lives.

Taking care of your breast health isn’t selfish. It’s an act of strength, love, and hope—for yourself and for everyone who loves you.

counterfactuals.output:
## Every Step Can Bring Us Closer to a Future Without Breast Cancer  
*By [Celebrity Name]*

Breast cancer has touched far too many of our lives. It is a diagnosis heard by our mothers, sisters, daughters, friends, colleagues—and people in our own homes. Behind every statistic is a person facing fear and uncertainty, supported by loved ones who would do anything to help.

That is why I am proud to support the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade and its commitment to improving access to breast cancer education, screening, treatment, and research. For decades, the Crusade has helped bring attention and resources to communities where care can be hardest to reach. That work matters because a person’s income, neighborhood, or background should never determine whether they receive timely, high-quality care.

We can all take an important first step by taking our breast health seriously. Know what is normal for your body, speak with a qualified health professional about any changes or concerns, and ask when clinical breast exams and mammograms are appropriate for you. Screening recommendations vary based on age, family history, genetics, and other risk factors, so make an informed plan with your healthcare provider. If you notice a new lump, skin or nipple changes, unusual discharge, or persistent pain, do not wait to seek medical advice.

But awareness alone is not enough. We must turn concern into action.

Upcoming Avon Walk events offer a powerful way to do exactly that. Each mile walked and every dollar raised can help expand education, support essential services, and advance efforts against breast cancer. You do not need to be an athlete or a medical expert to make a difference. You can walk, volunteer, donate, fundraise, or simply encourage someone else to participate.

I have seen what happens when people unite around a common purpose: strangers become teammates, survivors become sources of strength, and remembrance becomes resolve. The Avon Walk is more than a fundraising event. It is a public promise that no one should have to face breast cancer alone.

Please join me. Schedule the healthcare conversation you have been postponing. Encourage someone you love to do the same. Then sign up for an upcoming Avon Walk event—or support a participant—and help carry this movement forward.

Every exam is an act of self-care. Every conversation can raise awareness. Every step can help create change.

Together, let’s walk toward a future in which everyone has access to the information, screening, treatment, and hope they deserve.

*Visit [official campaign or event URL] for current Avon Walk dates, registration information, and ways to support the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade.*
